extracted.intended_audience: state policymakers, regulatory analysts, and policy researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and description of State RegData 2.0: what measures the dataset contains, how they are defined and calculated, data-collection limitations, and how policymakers and researchers can use the measures to evaluate state-level regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Cumulative volume of regulations measured in words (State RegData 2.0 reports 416 million words across analyzed state codes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word counts are comparable across states (unlike page counts, which vary by page/font size) and can be gathered from all rules. They provide a more consistent measure of regulatory volume than page counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory restrictions (restriction counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts of regulatory restrictions in administrative codes; State RegData reports 6.07 million regulatory restrictions total and state-level totals (e.g., California 395,608; Idaho 38,961).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory restrictions are instances of specific restrictive terms (see 'Definition of regulatory restriction terms'). Restriction counts are comparable across states and can be multiplied by industry-relevance probabilities to estimate industry-relevant restrictions. They are more comprehensive than selective cost-benefit estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of regulatory restriction terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory restrictions are instances of the terms 'shall,' 'must,' 'may not,' 'prohibited,' and 'required' in regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explicit term list defines what the dataset counts as a restriction; using a consistent list enables comparability across states and time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry relevance (industry-relevant restrictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability that a portion of regulatory text is relevant to a particular industry; industries are identified using the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) at the three-digit level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Industry-relevant restrictions are estimated by multiplying the industry-relevance probability for a text portion by the number of regulatory restrictions in that portion. Version 2.0 uses an improved industry classifier; examples include NAICS 561 (administrative and support services) and NAICS 541 (professional, scientific, and technical services).

rubrics_metrics.name: Average sentence length (complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Average sentence length in a code or section of code measured in number of words (used as a complexity metric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported as a complexity indicator (e.g., Arizona ~12 words/sentence = least complex; New York ~42 words/sentence = most complex by this measure). This metric was newly added in State RegData 2.0 to supplement volume measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shannon Entropy (complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shannon Entropy as a measure of the amount of information contained in regulatory text (used as a complexity metric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher entropy suggests a regulation includes more different kinds of information on average (e.g., South Carolina highest; South Dakota lowest). Entropy complements sentence-length and conditional-term measures to capture text complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of conditional terms (complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count of conditional terms in regulatory text as an indicator of complexity (one of the complexity measures added in 2.0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditional terms increase textual complexity and may indicate rules that are harder to interpret or apply; used together with sentence length and entropy to assess complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparability across states
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures (word counts, restriction counts, industry-relevant restrictions, complexity metrics) are defined so they are comparable across states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike page counts (which depend on fonts/page sizes) and selective agency cost-benefit reports, these counts are directly comparable across jurisdictions because they measure text and explicit term instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness of coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction and word counts can be gathered from all of the rules in place in a state's administrative code, providing comprehensive coverage of administrative regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This comprehensiveness contrasts with cost-benefit estimates that are usually drawn from a non-representative handful of regulations; comprehensive counts better represent the full regulatory system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete interpretability of metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory restrictions, word counts, and industry-relevant restrictions have clear, concrete meanings compared with more interpretive measures like net-benefit calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because these metrics are literal text-derived measures, they avoid some of the subjective interpretation inherent in cost-benefit reports, making them useful for tracking and comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope limitation: administrative codes only
rubrics_metrics.description: State RegData covers only administrative laws in state administrative codes; it does not include statutes, guidance documents, memoranda, or other policy documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users should remember that other layers of law exist and that the dataset does not capture those; future versions might expand coverage to include some of these materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-collection coverage and exclusion reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Several states were excluded from State RegData 2.0 for specific, documented technical or legal reasons (Arkansas, Hawaii, New Jersey, Vermont, Alaska, Connecticut for various reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion reasons include: no compiled administrative code (Arkansas), state sites linking to department pages requiring unique scrapers (Hawaii), third-party terms forbidding text downloading (LexisNexis for New Jersey and Vermont), website updates producing incomplete catalogs (Alaska), and sites blocking programmatic scraping after many pages (Connecticut). These constraints affect completeness and should be considered when comparing states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improved industry classifier and agency delineation (Version 2.0 improvements)
rubrics_metrics.description: State RegData 2.0 uses an improved industry classifier and more clearly delineates the agencies that write particular regulations compared with version 1.0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These improvements increase the precision of industry-relevance estimates and attribution of regulations to authorship, improving the dataset's usefulness for state-level analysis. Version 2.0 also required less time to collect because it reused prior infrastructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal precision / stock measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: State RegData 2.0 more precisely pinpoints the stock of state regulation that existed at a particular moment in time (codes collected March–June 2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because collection used more automated pipelines than v1.0, the dataset represents a snapshot of regulatory stock at collection time; users should consider timing when analyzing changes across versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for estimating industry/regulatory burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate industry-specific regulatory burden by aggregating industry-relevant restrictions across states (e.g., sum of estimated restrictions per NAICS 3-digit across states).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: NAICS 561 estimated to face 387,007 cumulative restrictions; NAICS 541 estimated 364,393. The method relies on multiplying relevance probabilities by restriction counts and aggregating across jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy-use criteria for tracking regulatory reform
rubrics_metrics.description: State RegData metrics can be used by policymakers to set and measure regulatory-reform targets (e.g., measure baseline, set reduction targets, track percent change in restrictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of use: Missouri and Idaho cited RegData when claiming reductions in restrictions (Idaho reported 37% reduction; Missouri 30%). The brief notes that successful reduction efforts typically include a concrete measure of regulation, an estimated baseline, and a reduction target—elements absent in some reviews (e.g., Maryland).
